car-pooling.pattern: Difference array (sweep line): +p at pickup, −p at drop-off, then a running sum

approaches.name: Check the load at every kilometre
approaches.idea: For each kilometre point, add up the passengers of every trip that is in the car there (`from ≤ x < to`).
steps: Let `K` be the largest drop-off point.
For each `x` in `[0, K)`: sum `passengers` over trips with `from ≤ x < to`.
If any sum exceeds `capacity`, return false.
approaches.why: K ≤ 1000 points × n trips. The half-open `to` means people leave before others board at the same point.

approaches.name: Sort pickup and drop-off events
approaches.idea: Turn each trip into two events, `(from, +p)` and `(to, −p)`. Sort by position, with drop-offs before pickups at the same point, and keep a running load.
steps: Create 2n events and sort by position, then by delta (negative first).
Walk the events adding the delta; if the load ever exceeds `capacity`, return false.
approaches.why: Dominated by sorting; works for any coordinate range.

approaches.name: Difference array over the kilometres
approaches.idea: Since positions are at most 1000, record `+p` at `from` and `−p` at `to` in an array; the prefix sum at each point is the load there.
steps: `diff[from] += p`, `diff[to] −= p` for every trip.
Walk `diff` with a running sum; if it exceeds `capacity`, return false.
approaches.why: K = 1001 positions; no sorting. At a shared point the drop-off and pickup cancel within the same cell, matching the rules.

range-sum-query-mutable.pattern: Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree): point update + prefix sum in O(log n)

approaches.name: Plain array
approaches.idea: Store the array; update writes one cell, and a range sum loops over the range.
steps: `update(i, v)`: `nums[i] = v`.
`sumRange(l, r)`: add `nums[l..r]`.
approaches.why: O(1) updates but O(n) per query, so 10⁵ queries on 10⁵ elements is 10¹⁰ steps.

approaches.name: Square-root decomposition
approaches.idea: Split the array into blocks of about √n elements and keep each block's sum. A query adds whole blocks in the middle and single elements at the two ragged ends.
steps: Block size `b = ⌈√n⌉`; `blocks[k]` = sum of block k.
`update(i, v)`: adjust `blocks[i / b]` by `v − nums[i]`, then set `nums[i]`.
`sumRange(l, r)`: while `l ≤ r`, add a whole block when `l` starts one that fits, otherwise add `nums[l]` and step by one.
approaches.why: O(1) updates and O(√n) queries: at most 2√n single elements plus √n blocks.

approaches.name: Fenwick tree
approaches.idea: A Fenwick tree stores partial sums so that both "add to one position" and "sum of a prefix" touch only O(log n) cells, by jumping along the lowest set bit (`i & −i`). A range sum is the difference of two prefix sums.
steps: Build: for each `i` (1-based), add `tree[i]` into `tree[i + (i & −i)]` — O(n).
`update(i, v)`: `delta = v − nums[i]`; for `j = i + 1` while `j ≤ n`: `tree[j] += delta`, `j += j & −j`.
`prefix(k)`: for `j = k` while `j > 0`: add `tree[j]`, `j −= j & −j`.
`sumRange(l, r) = prefix(r + 1) − prefix(l)`.
approaches.why: Both operations walk at most log₂ n levels. A segment tree achieves the same bounds with more code.

count-of-smaller-numbers-after-self.pattern: Scan from the right with a Fenwick tree over values (or merge-sort counting)

approaches.name: Count to the right of each element
approaches.idea: For each element, scan everything after it and count the smaller values.
steps: For each `i`, count `j > i` with `nums[j] < nums[i]`.
Store the count in `result[i]`.
approaches.why: About n²/2 comparisons — 5·10⁹ for n = 10⁵.

approaches.name: Sorted list built from the right
approaches.idea: Walk from right to left keeping the values seen so far in sorted order. The number of smaller values to the right is the insertion position of the current value, found by binary search.
steps: For `i` from n − 1 down to 0: `pos` = first index in `sorted` with value ≥ `nums[i]`.
`result[i] = pos`; insert `nums[i]` at `pos`.
approaches.why: The binary search is O(log n) but inserting into an array shifts up to n elements. It is fast in practice (a memory move), yet the worst case stays quadratic.

approaches.name: Fenwick tree over values, scanning from the right
approaches.idea: Shift values into 1..20001 (they lie in −10⁴..10⁴). Walking right to left, the Fenwick tree holds counts of values already seen; the answer for `nums[i]` is the prefix count of strictly smaller values.
steps: `OFFSET = 10001`, so `v = nums[i] + OFFSET` is in `[1, 20001]`.
For `i` from n − 1 down to 0: `result[i] = prefix(v − 1)`; then `add(v, 1)`.
approaches.why: V = 20001 possible values, so each step is about 15 tree hops. For unbounded values, compress coordinates first; merge sort that counts right-half elements overtaking each left element also gives O(n log n).

reverse-pairs.pattern: Merge-sort counting: count cross pairs between two sorted halves with a moving pointer

approaches.name: Check every pair
approaches.idea: Test `nums[i] > 2·nums[j]` for every `i < j`, in 64-bit arithmetic.
steps: For every `i < j`: if `nums[i] > 2·nums[j]` (as a 64-bit value), count it.
Return the count.
approaches.why: About 1.25·10⁹ pairs for n = 5·10⁴.

approaches.name: Sorted list of earlier values + binary search
approaches.idea: Walk left to right keeping earlier values sorted. For `nums[j]`, the earlier values greater than `2·nums[j]` are everything after its upper bound.
steps: For each `j`: `count += size − upperBound(sorted, 2·nums[j])`.
Insert `nums[j]` at its sorted position.
approaches.why: Searches are O(log n), but each array insertion can shift O(n) elements.

approaches.name: Merge sort with a counting pass
approaches.idea: Sort recursively. Before merging two sorted halves, count pairs with `i` in the left half and `j` in the right: as `nums[i]` grows, the set of `j` with `nums[i] > 2·nums[j]` only grows, so one forward pointer counts them all.
steps: Recursively sort and count each half.
For each `i` in the left half, advance `j` in the right half while `nums[i] > 2·nums[j]`; add `j − (mid + 1)`.
Merge the two halves as usual.
approaches.why: Each level does a linear count plus a linear merge, over log n levels. `2L·nums[j]` (64-bit) avoids overflow at the int extremes.

count-of-range-sum.pattern: Prefix sums + merge-sort counting of pairs whose difference lies in [lower, upper]

approaches.name: Sum every subarray
approaches.idea: Fix the start, extend the end one element at a time keeping a running 64-bit sum, and count sums inside the range.
steps: For each `i`: `sum = 0`; for each `j ≥ i`: `sum += nums[j]`; count it if `lower ≤ sum ≤ upper`.
Return the count.
approaches.why: n(n + 1)/2 subarrays, O(1) each.

approaches.name: Sorted prefix sums + binary search
approaches.idea: With prefix sums `P`, a subarray `(i, j]` qualifies when `P[j] − upper ≤ P[i] ≤ P[j] − lower`. Keep earlier prefix sums sorted and count that window with two binary searches.
steps: Start with `sorted = [0]` (the empty prefix).
For each new prefix sum `p`: count values in `[p − upper, p − lower]` via lower/upper bounds.
Insert `p` at its sorted position.
approaches.why: Counting is O(log n), but array insertion shifts up to n elements; a balanced tree with subtree sizes would make this O(n log n).

approaches.name: Merge sort over prefix sums
approaches.idea: Merge sort the prefix-sum array. Before merging two sorted halves, for each left value `P[i]` find the window of right values with `lower ≤ P[j] − P[i] ≤ upper`. Both window edges only move forward as `P[i]` grows.
steps: Build `P[0..n]` with `P[0] = 0` (64-bit).
In each merge step, for each `i` in the left half: advance `lo` while `P[lo] − P[i] < lower`, advance `hi` while `P[hi] − P[i] ≤ upper`; add `hi − lo`.
Merge the halves and return the total.
approaches.why: Linear work per level over log n levels. Prefix sums reach ±2·10¹⁴, so they need 64-bit integers (JavaScript doubles are exact up to 2⁵³).

create-sorted-array-through-instructions.pattern: Fenwick tree over values: count strictly less and strictly greater in O(log V)

approaches.name: Count by scanning every earlier value
approaches.idea: For each insertion, scan all values inserted so far and count those strictly less and strictly greater.
steps: For each `i`, count `j < i` with `instructions[j] < x` and with `instructions[j] > x`.
Add the smaller count to the total (mod 10⁹ + 7).
approaches.why: About n²/2 comparisons — 5·10⁹ for n = 10⁵.

approaches.name: Keep the container sorted, binary search
approaches.idea: Actually maintain the sorted container. Lower bound gives the count of strictly smaller values; size minus upper bound gives the strictly greater ones.
steps: For each `x`: `less = lowerBound(x)`, `greater = size − upperBound(x)`.
Add `min(less, greater)`; insert `x` at `lowerBound(x)`.
approaches.why: Searches are O(log n) but array insertion can shift O(n) elements each time.

approaches.name: Fenwick tree of value counts
approaches.idea: Values are at most 10⁵, so keep a Fenwick tree of how many times each value has been inserted. Before inserting the i-th value `x`: `less = prefix(x − 1)` and `greater = i − prefix(x)`.
steps: Tree over values 1..max.
For the i-th value `x` (0-based count `i` already inserted): `less = prefix(x − 1)`, `greater = i − prefix(x)`.
Add `min(less, greater)` to the total mod 10⁹ + 7; then `add(x, 1)`.
approaches.why: Two prefix queries and one update per value, each about 17 hops for V = 10⁵.

falling-squares.pattern: Interval max + assign: brute-force overlap checks, or a segment tree over compressed coordinates

approaches.name: Compare with every landed square
approaches.idea: A new square `[left, left + side)` rests on the tallest earlier square it overlaps (touching edges do not count). Its top is that height plus `side`.
steps: Keep each landed square as `(left, right, top)`.
For a new square, `base` = the max `top` over earlier squares with `l < right` and `left < r`.
Its top is `base + side`; append it and record the running maximum.
approaches.why: Each square checks all earlier ones; with n ≤ 1000 that is only 5·10⁵ checks, so this is the common interview answer.

approaches.name: Segment tree over compressed coordinates
approaches.idea: Compress all square edges to indices; cell `k` stands for `[xs[k], xs[k + 1])`. Each drop is a range-max query over its cells followed by raising those cells to `max + side`. Because the new height exceeds everything in the range, "assign" is the same as "raise to at least", which a lazy max-tag handles.
steps: Collect every `left` and `left + side`, sort and deduplicate into `xs`; there are `xs.length − 1` cells.
For a square, its cells are `[index(left), index(left + side) − 1]`.
`h = queryMax(cells) + side`; `chmax(cells, h)` with lazy propagation.
Record the running maximum of `h`.
approaches.why: Each query and update touches O(log n) nodes of a tree over at most 2n coordinates. Using half-open cells makes squares that only touch at an edge share no cell.
